questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.hint: A slice x[a:b] starts at index a and stops BEFORE index b. Python counts from 0.
questions.explain: Indexes 1, 2, 3 are selected (the stop index 4 is not included), so the result is [20, 30, 40].

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
print([n * n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0])
questions.hint: Read it from the right: first the loop, then the condition that filters, and only then the expression at the front.
questions.explain: Only the even numbers 2 and 4 pass the if-filter. Each one is squared: 2×2 = 4 and 4×4 = 16 → [4, 16]. [1, 9] squares the ODD numbers instead.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.hint: When you do not pass b, Python uses its default value. When you do pass it, the default is ignored.
questions.explain: price(3) uses the default b = 2, so 3 × 2 = 6. price(3, 4) uses b = 4, so 3 × 4 = 12.

questions.q: Which line shows how many missing values each column of df has?
questions.hint: Think in two steps: mark which cells are missing, then ADD UP those marks for each column. Which option does both?
questions.explain: df.isna() gives a True/False table and .sum() adds the True values (True = 1) per column. .count() counts every row, missing or not, so it just gives the number of rows. .mean() gives the SHARE missing, not the count.

questions.q: df has the columns age and city. Which line keeps only people older than 30 who live in Tashkent?
questions.hint: Check three details in each option: the sign pandas uses for AND, the brackets around each condition, and = versus ==.
questions.explain: pandas combines conditions with & (the word and raises an error on a Series), each condition needs its own ( ) because & runs before > and ==, and a comparison uses == (a single = is assignment).

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.hint: Split the rows by city first. Then decide what the summary function does to each small group: add, take the first, or something else?
questions.explain: City A has sales 10 and 30, mean = 20. City B has 20 and 40, mean = 30. 40/60 would be .sum(), 10/20 .first(), and 30/40 .max().

questions.q: Which line fills the missing values in the column age with the median of that column?
questions.hint: Three things to check: which method FILLS, which function gives the MIDDLE value, and does the line SAVE its result back into df?
questions.explain: fillna fills, median() gives the middle value, and assigning back to df["age"] keeps the result. mean() is the average, dropna removes rows, and a line without df["age"] = in front throws the result away (the last option has both mistakes).

questions.q: Before any threshold is applied, what does the output of logistic regression look like?
options: Any real number, like a price
questions.hint: An S-shaped function squeezes the model's raw score into a fixed range. Which range makes sense for 'how likely is class 1?'
questions.explain: Logistic regression passes its score through the sigmoid function, which gives a value between 0 and 1. A threshold (usually 0.5) then turns it into a class label.

questions.q: A logistic regression flags a customer as 'will churn' when probability ≥ 0.5. The company lowers the threshold to 0.3. What usually happens?
options: The same customers are flagged, because the model weights do not change
More customers are flagged, so precision rises and recall usually falls
Fewer customers are flagged, so precision rises and recall usually falls
More customers are flagged, so recall rises and precision usually falls
questions.hint: It is easier to pass a lower bar. If more customers pass, think about how many real churners you catch, and how many wrong flags you add.
questions.explain: A lower threshold labels more cases as positive. You catch more real churners (recall up) but also add false alarms (precision usually down). The weights stay the same, but the predicted classes change.

questions.q: A bank tests a fraud model on 1,000 transactions: 950 are normal and 50 are fraud. The model predicts "normal" for every transaction, so accuracy is 95%. Which number shows the model is useless?
options: Accuracy on the whole test set: 95%
questions.hint: A high score can hide a model that never finds the rare class. Count how many of the 50 fraud cases it found.
questions.explain: The model found 0 of the 50 fraud cases, so fraud recall is 0%. The other numbers all look good only because 95% of the data is the normal class.

questions.q: An email spam filter must avoid sending real emails to the spam folder. Which metric matters most?
questions.hint: Think about the mistake that hurts most: a real email called spam. Is that a false alarm or a miss? Then pick the metric that punishes that kind of error.
questions.explain: Precision = of all emails called spam, how many really were spam. A real email in the spam folder is a false positive, and precision drops when false positives increase.

questions.q: A hospital model screens for a serious disease. Missing a sick patient is much worse than a false alarm. Which metric should the team focus on?
questions.hint: Which error is worse here: a healthy person flagged, or a sick person missed? Choose the metric that counts the worse error.
questions.explain: Recall = of all really sick patients, how many did the model find. A missed patient is a false negative, and recall drops when false negatives increase.

questions.q: Using this confusion matrix, what is the recall of the Positive class?
questions.hint: Recall looks only at the REAL positive cases. Find that row in the matrix, then ask how many of them the model got right.
questions.explain: The real positives are the top row: 40 + 10 = 50. The model found 40 of them, so recall = 40 / 50 = 0.80. (0.67 is the precision, 0.70 is the accuracy.)

questions.q: A model has TP = 30, FP = 10, FN = 20 and TN = 40. What is its precision?
questions.hint: Precision looks only at what the model CALLED positive. Which two numbers together make up 'called positive', and how many of those were right?
questions.explain: Called positive = TP + FP = 30 + 10 = 40. Correct ones = 30. Precision = 30 / 40 = 0.75. (0.60 is the recall, 0.70 is the accuracy, 0.80 is TN / (TN + FP).)

questions.q: A model has precision = 0.50 and recall = 1.00. What is its F1 score (rounded)?
questions.hint: F1 is not the ordinary average of the two scores. It stays low when one of them is low.
questions.explain: F1 is the harmonic mean: 2 × (0.50 × 1.00) / (0.50 + 1.00) = 1.00 / 1.50 ≈ 0.67. The simple average would be 0.75, but F1 punishes the weak precision.

questions.q: Look at the three plots. Which one shows linear regression?
questions.hint: Linear regression predicts a number. Compare the SHAPE of each fitted line and the kind of values on each y-axis.
questions.explain: Plot X fits one straight line through numeric data: linear regression. Plot Y is an S-curve on 0/1 classes (logistic regression). Plot Z is a staircase, typical for a decision tree regressor, so 'X and Z' is wrong.

questions.q: What do the dashed vertical segments between the points and the line represent?
options: The decision boundary between the two classes
The residuals: actual value minus predicted value
The slope of the fitted line at each data point
The spread of y values around their own mean
questions.hint: Each segment connects a real point to the line's prediction for the same x. What does that gap measure?
questions.explain: The gap between the actual y and the predicted y is the residual (error). MSE, RMSE and MAE are all built from these gaps.

questions.q: A model predicts house price from size, number of rooms and age of the building, using one straight-line equation. What is this called?
questions.hint: Two checks: is the target a number or a class, and how many input features are there?
questions.explain: Price is a number, so it is linear (not logistic). With several features (size, rooms, age) it is MULTIPLE linear regression. Simple uses only one feature.

questions.q: Model A makes many small mistakes. Model B makes a few huge mistakes. Which metric punishes Model B's huge mistakes more strongly?
options: MSE, because it squares each error before averaging
Neither, because MSE and MAE give the same ranking
R², because it compares the model with the mean
MAE, because it averages the absolute size of errors
questions.hint: Compare an error of 10 with an error of 1 under each formula. Which formula makes the big error count far more than 10 times bigger?
questions.explain: MSE squares each error, so one error of 10 counts as 100, not 10. MAE treats big and small errors in proportion, and MSE and MAE can rank models differently.

questions.q: A linear regression model has R² = 0.85. What does this mean?
options: It is 85% accurate, in the same way as a classifier
It explains about 85% of the variation in the target
About 85% of its predictions are exactly the true value
Its average error is 0.85 units of the target
questions.hint: R² compares your model with a very simple baseline that always predicts the average. Is it counting correct predictions, or comparing errors?
questions.explain: R² is the share of the target's variation that the model explains compared with always predicting the mean. Regression predictions are almost never exactly right, so accuracy-style wording is wrong.

questions.q: Your linear regression has 200 features and many of them are useless. Which regularization can shrink some coefficients to exactly zero, removing those features?
questions.hint: The two penalties differ in shape: one adds the absolute size of each weight, the other adds the squared size. Which one can push a weight all the way to zero?
questions.explain: Lasso's absolute-value penalty can set coefficients exactly to zero (feature selection). Ridge, even with a large alpha, only shrinks them toward zero. Ordinary least squares has no penalty.

questions.q: Do decision trees and random forests need feature scaling (like StandardScaler)?
options: Yes, both need it or the chosen splits will be wrong
No, a split only compares one feature to a threshold
Yes, but only when the features use different units
Only random forest, because it averages many trees
questions.hint: A tree asks questions like 'is age > 30?'. Would the same rows land on the same sides of a split if you multiplied age by 1000 and moved the threshold with it?
questions.explain: Trees split one feature at a time by a threshold. Scaling does not change the order of the values, so the same splits are found. Scaling matters for distance-based or gradient-based models, not trees or forests.

questions.q: A decision tree gets 100% accuracy on the training data but only 70% on the test data. Which change most directly helps?
options: Limit the tree with a smaller max_depth
Make the test set bigger with test_size
Remove max_depth so the tree grows deeper
questions.hint: 100% on training but much lower on new data means the tree memorized. How could you stop it from asking so many very specific questions?
questions.explain: A big train/test gap is overfitting. A smaller max_depth (or larger min_samples_leaf) keeps the tree simpler. Scaling does not affect trees, and a bigger test set only measures the problem, it does not fix it.

questions.q: Why is a random forest usually less overfitted than one deep decision tree?
options: It is one tree that is trained with a smaller learning rate
It builds trees one by one, each fixing the last one's errors
It averages many trees built on random rows and features
It removes the noisy rows from the data before training
questions.hint: Think of asking a crowd instead of asking one person. What would make each person in the crowd give a different opinion?
questions.explain: A random forest trains many trees on random bootstrap samples with random feature subsets, then averages or votes, so their different errors partly cancel. Building trees one by one to fix errors is boosting, a different method.

questions.q: What does Gini impurity measure at a node of a decision tree?
options: How many leaves grow under the node
How much the node adds to accuracy
How many samples reach the node
How mixed the classes are in the node
questions.hint: A split is good when each side becomes more 'clean'. What would it mean for a node to be clean, and which number could describe that?
questions.explain: Gini impurity is 0 when all samples in a node belong to one class, and larger when classes are mixed. The tree picks splits that reduce impurity the most.

questions.q: Which pair of algorithms can solve BOTH classification and regression problems?
questions.hint: Think about what a tree's leaf can hold: a class label or an average number. Which algorithms use leaves like that?
questions.explain: A tree leaf can output a majority class (classification) or an average value (regression), so Decision Tree and Random Forest do both. Linear Regression is regression only, and Logistic Regression is classification only.

questions.q: What does encoding do in a machine learning pipeline?
options: Turns categories into numbers a model can use
Fills each missing value with the column mean
Rescales numeric columns to the range 0 to 1
Removes the duplicate rows from the dataset
questions.hint: Think about a column full of words like 'red' and 'blue'. What must happen to those words before a model can calculate with them?
questions.explain: Encoding converts categorical columns into numbers (for example one-hot or label encoding). Rescaling, filling missing values and removing duplicates are other preprocessing steps.

questions.q: Look at the Color column before and after. Which encoding method produced the table on the right?
questions.hint: Count the columns before and after. What does each new column answer for a row, and which values can it hold?
questions.explain: One-hot encoding (pd.get_dummies) creates one 0/1 column per category, and each row has exactly one 1. Label and ordinal encoding keep a single column of integers; target encoding keeps one column of averages.

questions.q: A City column was converted to City_code as shown, and the result is given to a logistic regression. What is the main problem?
options: Integer codes make the model train much more slowly than text
The codes are too small, so MinMaxScaler must be applied first
Logistic regression cannot accept integer columns as its input
The model reads 2 as bigger than 0, an order cities do not have
questions.hint: Look at the numbers 0, 1, 2. A linear or logistic formula multiplies each feature by a weight. What does that do to how the values compare with each other?
questions.explain: Label encoding gives each city an arbitrary integer. Linear and logistic models read the numbers as ordered distances, so Tashkent (2) looks 'twice' Samarkand (1). For unordered categories, use one-hot encoding.

questions.q: You standardize features before training a logistic regression. What is the correct way to use StandardScaler with a train/test split?
options: Fit on the test set, then transform the train set with it
Fit on the full dataset, then transform train and test
Fit on train, fit again on test, then transform each one
Fit on the train set, then transform both train and test
questions.hint: The test set must behave like brand-new, unseen data. Which data is allowed to teach the scaler its mean and standard deviation?
questions.explain: The scaler must learn its mean and std from training data only. Fitting on the full data or on the test set leaks test information into training (data leakage).
